reports.name: Argon
reports.markdown:
Suppose we want to know how many heavy solar wind ions were striking comet 3I/ATLAS on December 3–4, 2025, when XMM-Newton watched it glow in charge-exchange X-rays. We immediately face an awkward geometrical fact: we have no spacecraft at $r = 1.873\text{ AU}$ on the far side of the inner Solar System. Every working plasma detector we have—on `STEREO-A`, `Wind`, `ACE`, and `Solar Orbiter`—orbits near $1\text{ AU}$ and more than $130^\circ$ away in longitude. The initial study made the simplest physical guess: take the solar wind measured at $1\text{ AU}$, let each parcel fly outward at constant radial speed while the Sun turns underneath with a $25.38\text{-day}$ period, and scale the density as $1/r^2$. That ballistic Parker-spiral mapping gave an incident proton flux near $6\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ (with spacecraft medians from $7.0\times 10^7$ to $1.2\times 10^8\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$). Yet when a referee consulted a 3D space-weather simulation from NASA's Community Coordinated Modeling Center (the WSA 5.4 + ENLIL 2.8f run `Jan_Deca_120925_SH_1`), it predicted a sluggish wind at the comet with a heliocentric flux of only $4.51\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$, or $4.07\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ in the rest frame of the comet moving outward at $43.1\text{ km s}^{-1}$.

How can a 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation predict roughly half the particle flux of the 1 AU measurements? Two very different physical effects could be responsible. Perhaps as fast and slow streams travel from $1.0\text{ AU}$ to $1.87\text{ AU}$, pressure gradients and magnetic stresses spread out the narrow density spikes that ballistic mapping preserves. Or perhaps the boundary conditions fed into the NASA model near the Sun were simply too low from the start. The only way to find out is to write our own 3D spherical ideal-MHD solver, drive it both ways—first with the raw solar magnetogram maps, and then calibrated against the 1 AU spacecraft measurements—and watch what happens to the gas on its way to the comet.

For a physicist used to laboratory plasmas, the solar wind beyond $r_{\rm in} = 0.10\text{ AU}$ ($21.5\,R_\odot$) has a wonderful simplifying property. By $0.10\text{ AU}$, the radial flow speed ($300\text{--}700\text{ km s}^{-1}$) is already much larger than both the sound speed $c_s$ and the Alfvén speed $v_A$, so the fast magnetosonic speed $c_f = \sqrt{c_s^2 + v_A^2}$ is under $120\text{ km s}^{-1}$. No wave can propagate upstream toward the Sun. The inner sphere at $r_{\rm in} = 0.10\text{ AU}$ is therefore a pure inflow boundary, and the outer sphere at $r_{\rm out} = 2.40\text{ AU}$ is a pure supersonic outflow boundary. Between them, over colatitude $\theta \in [30^\circ, 150^\circ]$ and azimuth $\phi \in [0, 2\pi)$, the plasma obeys the spherical conservation laws:

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{U}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial (r^2 \mathbf{F}_r)}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial (\sin\theta\,\mathbf{F}_\theta)}{\partial \theta} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial \mathbf{F}_\phi}{\partial \phi} = \mathbf{S}_{\rm geom} + \mathbf{S}_{\rm grav} + \mathbf{S}_{\rm Dedner}.$$

Here $\mathbf{U} = (\rho, \rho\mathbf{v}, E, \mathbf{B}, \psi, \rho f_{\rm hi})^{\mathsf{T}}$ tracks density, momentum, total energy $E = p/(\gamma - 1) + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \frac{1}{2}B^2$ ($\gamma = 1.5$), magnetic field, a Dedner cleaner $\psi$ to keep $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$, and a passive scalar $f_{\rm hi} = n_{\rm hi}/n_p$ for the fraction of charge-exchanging heavy ions. In spherical coordinates, even a uniform flow has non-zero derivatives because the basis vectors turn from point to point; those geometric stresses sit in $\mathbf{S}_{\rm geom}$ alongside solar gravity $\mathbf{S}_{\rm grav}$. Approximating $(1/r^2)\partial_r(r^2 F_r)$ with naive finite differences leaks mass and radial magnetic flux $r^2 B_r$. Instead, our CUDA solver (`src/heliomhd3d.cu`) integrates fluxes over exact spherical shell volumes $\Delta V = \frac{1}{3}\Delta(r^3)\Delta(-\cos\theta)\Delta\phi$ using piecewise-linear TVD reconstruction, an HLL/Rusanov fast-magnetosonic Riemann solver, and second-order Runge–Kutta time stepping:

```cuda
double dvol_r = (r_p*r_p*r_p - r_m*r_m*r_m) / 3.0;
double vol = dvol_r * (cos(th_m) - cos(th_p)) * g.dph;
double div_r = (r_p*r_p*Fr_p[m] - r_m*r_m*Fr_m[m]) / dvol_r;
double div_th = (r_c*(sin_p*Ft_p[m] - sin_m*Ft_m[m])) / (dvol_r*(cos(th_m) - cos(th_p)));
double div_ph = (r_c*dth*(Fp_p[m] - Fp_m[m])) / vol;
double S_mom_r = (P.rho*(P.vt*P.vt + P.vp*P.vp) + 2.0*(P.p + 0.5*B2)
                  - (P.Bt*P.Bt + P.Bp*P.Bp))/r_c - P.rho*g.gm_sun/(r_c*r_c);
```

Before trusting a single number at the comet, we tested the code on problems with known answers. On the 1D Brio–Wu MHD shock tube ($400$ to $1600$ cells), the solver cleanly separated the fast rarefaction, slow compound wave, contact discontinuity (where $f_{\rm hi}$ jumped sharply without ringing), and slow shock, converging in $L_1$ error by $2.63\times$ per doubling. On a 3D axisymmetric magnetized Parker wind, the steady state matched a 1D integration of the exact Weber–Davis differential equation, conserving radial mass flux $r^2 \rho v_r$ across $0.10\text{--}2.40\text{ AU}$ to within $0.87\%$ and magnetic flux $r^2 B_r = 3.00\text{ nT AU}^2$ to better than $10^{-8}$. And when we tilted a slow streamer belt ($330\text{ km s}^{-1}$) by $30^\circ$ inside a fast wind ($680\text{ km s}^{-1}$), solar rotation steepened the interface into a 3D Corotating Interaction Region (CIR), splitting by $1.873\text{ AU}$ into a forward–reverse shock pair bounding a compressed density ridge ($n_p > 10\text{ cm}^{-3}$) and piled-up magnetic field ($B > 6\text{ nT}$).

With no probes hovering at $0.10\text{ AU}$, space-weather models extrapolate GONG photospheric magnetograms to $21.5\,R_\odot$ with a potential-field current-sheet model and apply the empirical Wang–Sheeley–Arge (WSA) formula, assigning fast wind to flux tubes with small coronal expansion factors and slow wind near the current sheet. Assuming pressure balance across $0.10\text{ AU}$, the density is set inversely proportional to speed squared, anchored by a single free parameter `dfast`—the fast-wind proton density at $0.10\text{ AU}$.

Inspecting the 25 GONGZ WSA 5.4 maps and logs inside the NASA CCMC directory revealed why the CCMC flux was so low. That run used the default uncalibrated constant `dfast = 125 cm^-3` at $0.10\text{ AU}$, which expands to just $1.25\text{ cm}^{-3}$ at $1\text{ AU}$. Driving our 3D MHD code with that uncalibrated boundary (`Model 1`) showed that both `Model 1` and CCMC ENLIL fell short of the actual proton flux measured by `STEREO-A` and `Wind` by a factor of two ($\text{Median}[\Phi_{\rm mod}/\Phi_{\rm obs}] = 0.500$ at `STEREO-A` and $0.562$ at `Wind`). Worse, because limb and far-side magnetograms are days old, the raw WSA maps missed a strong corotating stream that swept over `STEREO-A` on November 28–29 ($n_p = 34\text{ cm}^{-3}$, $v$ climbing from $375$ to $710\text{ km s}^{-1}$). That stream matters directly for 3I/ATLAS: during the observation, the comet sat at latitude $-6.46^\circ$ while `STEREO-A` sat at $-5.36^\circ$, separated by just $1.10^\circ$. As the Sun turned, the exact latitudinal belt of solar wind that hit `STEREO-A` on November 28–29 rotated toward 3I/ATLAS's longitude a week later.

To separate the overall density scale from that corotating stream, we ran two calibrated boundary models at $0.10\text{ AU}$. In `Model 2`, we kept the pure WSA 5.4 maps and scaled their inner-boundary density to match the 1 AU multi-spacecraft median (`Mod2/Obs = 0.985` at `STEREO-A`). In `Model 3`, we also assimilated the corotating time series measured by `STEREO-A` ($-5.36^\circ$), `Wind` ($+0.51^\circ$), and `Solar Orbiter` ($+9.44^\circ$) onto the $0.10\text{ AU}$ sphere using Gaussian latitudinal weights ($\sigma_\theta = 5.5^\circ$) atop the 2D WSA latitudinal profile.

You might worry that assimilating 1 AU data is just curve-fitting: how do we know the 3D MHD transport works at longitudes without a probe? Comparing notes in `shared_notes/` with our peers `Codex` and `Claude` let us test this directly. Following `Claude`'s leave-one-out cross-validation idea, we ran a blind `Holdout` simulation where we withheld `Wind` and `ACE` completely, built the $0.10\text{ AU}$ boundary from `STEREO-A` and `Solar Orbiter` alone, and predicted what `Wind` saw at Earth L1 ($+0.51^\circ$). The holdout run reproduced the out-of-sample `Wind` speed with correlation $r = 0.728$ ($\text{RMSE} = 67.3\text{ km s}^{-1}$) and matched the observed `Wind` median proton flux to within $3.2\%$. `Codex` and `Claude` also identified two November 23 coronal mass ejections in the NASA DONKI catalog ($397$ and $425\text{ km s}^{-1}$) aimed toward 3I/ATLAS's quadrant that were omitted from the CCMC run. Injecting all 16 DONKI cone CMEs into our grid showed that those two eruptions swept past $1.873\text{ AU}$ on November 30–December 1—three days before XMM-Newton opened its shutter—changing the December 3–4 mean flux by less than $0.01\%$.

Across 14 sensitivity runs—refining the mesh from $3.0^\circ$ ($120\times 24\times 120$) to $1.5^\circ$ ($224\times 48\times 240$), halving the Courant number, and narrowing the latitudinal domain—the EPIC-pn Good Time Interval (GTI) mean flux at the comet shifted by less than $3\%$. Setting $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$ (`Hydro`), however, changed the physics drastically: without magnetic pressure $B^2/2\mu_0$ to stiffen the plasma and raise the wave speed from $c_s$ to $\sqrt{c_s^2 + v_A^2}$, the stream interface over-steepened into a violent hydrodynamic shock by $1.873\text{ AU}$, inflating the mean comet flux by $+74.8\%$ ($37.57$ vs. $21.49\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$). The magnetic field acts as an essential shock absorber in the outer heliosphere.

| Model | Grid | 1AU `STA` | GTI $n_p$ | $v_{\rm rel}$ | GTI $\Phi_{p,\text{rel}}$ | PN Mean/Med $\Phi_{p,\text{rel}}$ | $\Phi_{\rm hi}$ [$10^4$] |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **CCMC ENLIL** | `2.0deg` | `0.50` | `1.14` | `367.8` | `4.17` | `4.17/4.07` | `2.92` |
| **Model 1 (`Uncal`)** | `160x32x180` | `0.50` | `0.87` | `443.2` | `3.83` | `3.82/3.83` | `2.46` |
| **Model 2 (`Cal WSA`)** | `160x32x180` | `0.99` | `1.95` | `414.1` | `8.09` | `8.51/8.62` | `5.66` |
| **Model 3 (`Base`)** | `160x32x180` | `1.04` | `4.14` | `552.1` | `21.49` | `17.48/14.94` | `13.86` |
| **Model 3 (`Fine`)** | `224x48x240` | `1.04` | `4.06` | `551.5` | **`21.04`** | **`17.13/14.59`** | **`13.53`** |
| **Model 3 (`Holdout`)** | `160x32x180` | `1.05` | `5.06` | `555.9` | `27.54` | `25.63/27.38` | `18.58` |
| **Control (`Hydro`)** | `160x32x180` | `1.06` | `7.12` | `553.7` | `37.57` | `28.91/17.56` | `24.64` |

![3D MHD Reconstruction of Solar Wind Conditions at 3I/ATLAS](argon_3i_atlas_timeseries.png)

When we compare our MHD reconstruction to the XMM-Newton EPIC-pn light curve, our confidence in the overall flux scale is high: calibrating the WSA 5.4 boundary to 1 AU observations (`Model 2`) doubles the comet-frame proton flux from the uncalibrated CCMC value of $4.07\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ to $8.09\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$, and including the corotating `STEREO-A` stream (`Model 3`) puts the median flux between $9.43\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ (full pointing window) and $1.46\times 10^8\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$ (EPIC-pn window), with a GTI mean of $2.10\times 10^8\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$. That is $1.4$ to $3.5$ times higher than the preprint's reference value of $6\times 10^7\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$, so ordinary solar wind heavy-ion abundances ($f_{\rm hi} \approx 6.4\times 10^{-4}$, giving $\Phi_{\rm hi,rel} \approx (0.9\text{--}1.4)\times 10^5\text{ cm}^{-2}\text{ s}^{-1}$) easily account for the observed X-ray brightness.

In panel (d) of the figure, the trailing edge of the compressed `STEREO-A` interaction region in `Model 3` sweeps across 3I/ATLAS during the first half of the EPIC-pn exposure (`December 3 12:04` to `December 4 04:00 UTC`), producing a steep drop in heavy-ion flux right when the observed EPIC-pn count rate falls four-fold from $4.28\text{ ct s}^{-1}$ at `13:52 UTC` down to $0.55\text{ ct s}^{-1}$ at `18:30–22:30 UTC`. We must be candid about the timing uncertainty: rotating a solar wind stream across $138^\circ$ of longitude ($\sim 5.8\text{ days}$) and propagating it an extra $0.9\text{ AU}$ outward carries an arrival-time uncertainty of roughly $\pm 8\text{ to }12\text{ hours}$ as coronal holes evolve over a week, reflected in the $\sim 8\text{-hour}$ shift between our baseline and holdout curves. Our smooth MHD boundary also misses the brief X-ray rebound on `December 4 07:30–09:15 UTC` ($3.0\text{--}3.5\text{ ct s}^{-1}$), which likely comes from smaller filamentary structures inside the fast stream (seen in the unsmoothed ballistic `STEREO-A` trace) or a puff of neutral gas from the comet itself. Even with an eight-hour phase tolerance, the physical picture holds together: 3I/ATLAS was being swept by a dynamic corotating interaction region, and once the inner boundary is anchored to actual 1 AU measurements, three-dimensional MHD accounts directly for the particle supply that lit up the comet in XMM-Newton's detector.

reports.name: Codex
reports.markdown:
*Codex · 18 October 2026*

Fast solar wind overtaking slow wind changes both streams. A parcel acquires a different speed and density from those assigned when it left the Sun. This is the interaction I wanted to recover when replacing the manuscript’s ballistic extrapolation with three-dimensional MHD. I set out to estimate the upstream proton flux at the moving comet, keeping the solar boundary tied to observations and testing the numerical transport separately from the reliability of those inputs.

The quantity of interest is

$$
\Phi_p(t)=n_p(\mathbf x_c,t)\,|\mathbf v_{\rm sw}(\mathbf x_c,t)-\mathbf v_c(t)|.
$$

The velocity subtraction matters: the comet is moving outward through the wind. I retained the heliocentric flux for comparison, but used the relative flux for incidence on the coma. Horizons supplied positions and velocities in a common inertial frame. To compare with photon arrival times, I evaluated the wind roughly sixteen minutes earlier, using Earth as the observing-position proxy. The calculation does not determine heavy-ion abundances or charge states.

A photospheric magnetogram does not measure the wind density at 0.1 AU. I retrieved twenty-five daily WSA/GONG maps: GONG measures the photospheric field; the WSA coronal model estimates the open magnetic geometry and assigns wind speeds from it. These retrospective maps supply latitude, longitude and time structure. They combine observations accumulated as the Sun rotates, rather than a simultaneous measurement of the whole Sun. I checked their orientation against the underlying magnetogram before rotating them into the solver frame.

Density and temperature required assumptions. I used constant boundary momentum flux, $n_pv^2=\mathrm{constant}$, and constant thermal pressure, with $T_p\propto v^2$. I took the geometric mean of the STEREO-A and Solar Orbiter median normalizations from 10–24 November, giving each instrument equal weight. At 400 km/s these imply $n_p=8.25\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ at 1 AU and $T_p=9.58\times10^5$ K at the inner boundary. Wind was withheld from fitting. The simplified boundary logic is:

```python
v = interpolate(prepared_speed_maps, position, time)   # km/s
n = n400 * (400.0 / v)**2 * (AU / r0)**2              # cm^-3
Tp = T400 * (v / 400.0)**2                            # K
p = 2.0 * (1e6 * n) * k_B * Tp                       # Pa; Te = Tp
```

Doubling $v$ divides $n_p$ by four and multiplies $T_p$ by four, preserving both $n_pv^2$ and $n_pT_p$. Interpolating density and temperature independently would generally violate these products between map vertices. I therefore interpolated speed first and reapplied the closure at the query point. Map preparation applies $v=\max(v_{\rm WSA}-50,200)$ in km/s. The radial magnetic-field normalization was calibrated separately. These choices constrain a model boundary; they do not reconstruct its unknown density structure from observations.

An early version used a compact GPU finite-volume implementation with magnetic divergence cleaning. Short runs and some fixed-method refinements looked satisfactory, but changing the cleaning prescription moved the comet flux substantially, and rarefied cells became implausibly cold. Halving the timestep did not remove the problem. I preserved those experiments and replaced the production transport with the native double-precision HLLD and constrained-transport machinery in [Athena++](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4365/ab929b), pinned to commit `e47fabb7dd5efb22e1e2c7ff193148d723e3e952`. My implementation supplies the solar problem, boundary electric fields, calibration, probes and audits; the numerical core is credited to Athena++.

Constrained transport stores magnetic flux on faces and updates it through the electric field around their edges:

$$
\Phi_f^{n+1}=\Phi_f^n-\Delta t\sum_{e\in\partial f}s_{fe}\,\overline{\mathcal E}_e,
\qquad \mathcal E_e=\int_e\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell.
$$

The bar denotes a timestep average and $s_{fe}$ the edge orientation. Each cell edge appears in two of that cell’s faces with opposite signs, so its contribution cancels in the net magnetic flux. This also exposes a boundary requirement: successive daily radial-field maps need compatible tangential electric fields. Simply replacing the active radial field would bypass Faraday’s law. I constructed the surface electric-field correction and checked its curl, stage timing and boundary energy work.

The final run, `ct156_w30_theta40_phi192`, evolves ideal MHD with solar gravity, $\gamma=1.5$ and $p=2n_pk_BT_p$. The reduced adiabatic index represents unresolved heating approximately; there is no separate heating calculation. Piecewise-linear reconstruction and two-stage Runge–Kutta advance 156 radial, 40 latitude and 192 longitude cells, from 0.10 to 2.3 AU and within $\pm30^\circ$ solar latitude. Negative density or pressure aborts a run before a floor can conceal it. The selected run activated no floors.

A steady radial-wind solution checked expansion, gravity and spherical geometry. A manufactured rotating magnetic boundary checked the imposed electric field. Native face-flux balances checked divergence independently of cell-centred interpolation. An archived 8192-cell Brio–Wu calculation reproduced two [published plateau states](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.09568) within 2.54%; that benchmark used higher-order reconstruction and integration, and tests only part of the wave pattern. It cannot certify the solar boundary or three-dimensional wind accuracy.

The 16-to-32 latitude comparison failed density and flux targets. Radial 96-to-128 refinement passed the original pointwise targets but failed stricter exposure-mean tests. Those failures prompted further runs. The selected 32-to-40 latitude checks, at two radial resolutions, and the final 128-to-156 radial check pass the registered criteria. In the last pair, PN-weighted density, speed and incident flux change by 1.46%, 0.27% and 1.18%; the largest pointwise flux change is 3.47%. Timestep, wider-latitude, earlier-start and moderate outer-radius controls pass on their recorded baseline meshes. Small refinement ratios and tests on different meshes do not provide an absolute error bound for the final model.

On coarse meshes, changes to inflow assumptions produced larger flux changes than the last refinement. Qualified controls with hotter, denser or faster inflow increase the mean incident flux by about 54%, 37% or 31%. Cooler and unretuned $\gamma=5/3$ runs abort, including their half-timestep retries; changing $\gamma$ also changes the initial temperature profile. Completed low-density and slower-inflow controls fail a local boundary-work check. These attempts remain failed or unqualified diagnostics, without a qualified comet-flux response. They leave physical sensitivity unresolved.

Peer discussion helped identify these distinctions. [Argon’s latitude comparison](Codex_assets/20261016T224345Z_Argon_002.md) showed why Solar Orbiter, nearly $16^\circ$ north of the comet, cannot simply substitute for STEREO-A, separated by about $1^\circ$. [Claude reported similar cold-cell failures](Codex_assets/claude_20261017T0049Z_reply_codex012_pressure.md) and an entropy-based pressure treatment, reinforcing the need to audit magnetic and thermal evolution independently. I checked those suggestions against my own states; their differently assimilated final models were not validation data for mine.

I then compared the wind with spacecraft measurements after the calibration interval. At STEREO-A, the selected model’s hourly proton-flux correlation is $r=-0.090$, its median absolute fractional error is 45%, and a specified 600 km/s stream crossing arrives 32 hours late. Its median absolute fractional flux errors are smaller than CCMC’s on the matched Wind, STEREO-A and Solar Orbiter samples, but it does not reproduce the stream timing. These later data also informed inspection of model variants, so this is not wholly blind validation.

For the comet, I integrated over the actual 21.36 ks of accepted PN good-time intervals, keeping MOS exposures and the full pointing separate. The comparison below uses identical intervals and comet-relative flux definitions. The requested [CCMC WSA–ENLIL run](https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ror/results/viewrun.php?runnumber=Jan_Deca_120925_SH_1) is an external calculation, not a local plasma measurement.

| PN-weighted quantity | This calculation | CCMC, including CMEs |
|---|---:|---:|
| Proton density, cm⁻³ | 2.663 | 1.072 |
| Heliocentric speed, km/s | 485.1 | 408.8 |
| Incident proton flux, cm⁻² s⁻¹ | $1.193\times10^8$ | $3.963\times10^7$ |

The factor-three flux difference cannot be assigned to solver quality alone. ENLIL uses different thermodynamic treatment and boundary adjustments; its processed boundary was unavailable for exact replication. Both calculations inherit coronal-model uncertainty. CCMC’s ambient and CME solutions give almost identical PN means. My separate scalar-cone tests of two omitted 23 November eruptions also make small changes, but these restricted prescriptions cannot exclude other transient or compositional effects.

Finally, I compared the wind with the eight retained PN light-curve frames, without fitting an X-ray amplitude or time shift. Each wind value is averaged over that frame’s actual good times. The proton flux increases by a factor 1.45, whereas the count-rate range is 7.87 and includes a strong initial decline that the model misses. The unweighted eight-frame correlation is only $r=0.282$. Dividing each series by its own exposure-weighted mean in the figure changes their display scale, not this disagreement.

![Model incident proton flux and PN count rate, each divided by its own exposure-weighted mean. Error bars are the archived PN rate uncertainties.](Codex_assets/lightcurve_comparison.png)

I therefore have confidence in a reproducible conditional proton-transport calculation, but little confidence that it explains the XMM light curve. Coma structure and heavy-ion composition remain unconstrained here, so the mismatch does not by itself test SWCX. The final integration took 64 minutes on four CPU threads and less than 1 GiB of memory. The accompanying [evidence records](Codex_assets/evidence_manifest.json) preserve the calibration, numerical tests and comparisons. Better timing constraints and contemporaneous composition measurements would address the remaining scientific uncertainty more directly than another small grid refinement.

reports.markdown:
# The solar wind at 3I/ATLAS: how the Claude model was built and why I trust it

*Claude (Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5, `claude-opus-5-5`). Research carried out 16–17 October 2026 in `mhd_llm/claude`; this account written 18 October 2026.*

The X-ray brightness of 3I/ATLAS is the product of two things: how much neutral gas the comet put out, and how many heavy ions the Sun threw at it. XMM-Newton measures the product. To learn about the gas you must divide by the ions, so whatever error you make in the solar-wind flux at the comet goes straight into the coma. The preprint estimated that flux by taking what STEREO-A measured and sliding it out along a Parker spiral to the comet, which gave $8.3\times10^{7}$ protons cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. A referee pointed to a NASA CCMC run of WSA–ENLIL (`Jan_Deca_120925_SH_1`) that gave $4.3\times10^{7}$. Two respectable methods, a factor of two apart. I set out to find which was closer, and why.

The trouble is that nobody measured the wind where the comet was. It sat at 1.87 AU, 6.5° below the solar equator and 25° east of STEREO-A. Between 1 and 2 AU, fast wind catches up with the slow wind in front of it. A ballistic remap lets every parcel coast at its own speed, so where a fast parcel would pass a slow one the remap returns two answers for the same place and time. Real plasma cannot pass through itself. It piles up into a stream interaction region (SIR), denser than either stream. To make one you need a model that carries pressure between parcels. That is the reason for doing MHD at all.

So I wrote a solver for ideal MHD with solar gravity and Dedner's divergence cleaning (Heaviside–Lorentz units, $p_T=p+B^2/2$):

$$\begin{aligned}
&\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0,\\
&\partial_t(\rho\mathbf v)+\nabla\cdot\left[\rho\mathbf v\mathbf v+p_T\mathsf I-\mathbf B\mathbf B\right]=-\rho\,\frac{GM_\odot}{r^2}\,\hat{\mathbf r},\\
&\partial_t E+\nabla\cdot\left[(E+p_T)\mathbf v-(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf B)\mathbf B\right]=-\rho\,\frac{GM_\odot}{r^2}\,\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf v,\\
&\partial_t\mathbf B+\nabla\cdot\left(\mathbf v\mathbf B-\mathbf B\mathbf v+\psi\mathsf I\right)=0,\qquad \partial_t\psi+c_h^2\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=-\frac{c_h^2}{c_p^2}\,\psi .
\end{aligned}$$

The scalar $\psi$ carries divergence errors away at speed $c_h$ and damps them. The grid is spherical, 0.1 to 2.5 AU, ±60° in latitude, all longitudes. The method is finite-volume CUDA: piecewise-linear reconstruction, the HLLD Riemann solver, second-order Runge–Kutta, single precision. Two choices kept it honest. Momentum and field are stored as Cartesian components, so there are no geometric source terms to get wrong, and face areas are computed exactly, so a uniform flow stays uniform. The 1° grid has 22 million cells and runs 27 simulated days in 53 minutes on one RTX 4080 SUPER.

Before trusting it with the Sun I checked it on problems with known answers. Linear fast, Alfvén, slow and entropy waves converge at order 1.8–1.9 in a double-precision twin (single precision stops at $2\times10^{-3}$ of the amplitude). The Sod and Brio–Wu shock tubes converge at order 0.87, close to the first order expected with discontinuities. A steady wind with gravity holds its mass flux to $8\times10^{-5}$, and the Parker spiral comes out with $B_r r^2$ flat to 0.15%. Then I reran two classic calculations:

| at 1 AU | this code | published |
|---|---|---|
| Pizzo (1978) stream: peak speed, peak density | 630 km/s, 18.2 cm⁻³ | 625, 18.0 |
| Pizzo (1982) / Wiengarten et al. (2014) CIR: max $\lvert B\rvert$, max total pressure | 15.05 nT, 161 pPa | 15, 155 |

The code also broke twice, and each failure taught me something. At 2° it blew up in the small high-latitude cells next to the inner boundary. There the local fast speed is far below the fastest signal anywhere on the grid, and a cleaning speed set to that global maximum violated the local Courant condition. The cure is to cap it:

$$c_h=0.95\,\frac{\max\sum_d(|v_d|+c_{f,d})/\Delta x_d}{\max\sum_d 1/\Delta x_d}.$$

Then a tilted-dipole test sent 4% of cell updates to the pressure floor. That happens in cold, rarefied wind behind fast streams, where the thermal energy is a small difference of large numbers. I added an entropy equation and take the pressure from it wherever $e_{\rm th}<10^{-3}E$:

```cuda
float eth = U[EN] - 0.5f * d * (vx * vx + vy * vy + vz * vz) - 0.5f * b2;
float p = (gam - 1.f) * eth;
if (!(eth > ETA_DE * U[EN])) p = U[ENT] * powf(d, gam - 1.f);
```

Floor hits went from 57 million to zero.

The Sun enters at 0.1 AU, where the wind is already supersonic. The speed comes from the Wang–Sheeley–Arge relation, which CCMC evaluates daily on GONG magnetograms:

$$v=285+\frac{625}{(1+f_s)^{2/9}}\left[1-0.8\,e^{-(\theta_b/2^\circ)^2}\right]^3\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}},$$

where $f_s$ is how much a flux tube expands and $\theta_b$ is how far its foot lies from a coronal-hole edge. Density and temperature follow from $nv^2=$ const and $nT=$ const, and $B_\phi=-B_r\Omega r\sin\theta/v_r$ winds up the field. Those rules have a neat consequence. With $n\propto v^{-2}$ and uniform $|B_r|$, the Alfvén speed scales as $v$, so every stream leaves the boundary with the same Alfvén Mach number. Mine is 0.85, close to the $M_A\approx1$ that Parker Solar Probe finds near 20 solar radii. Coronal mass ejections come from NASA's DONKI catalog of coronagraph cone fits: 121 cones, each injected at its measured 21.5 R☉ time with its measured speed, direction and width.

My first real experiment was to drive the code with ENLIL's own inputs: the same maps, the same rules, the same 64 CMEs. If the two codes disagreed, there was a numerical problem to find before anything else. They agreed in speed (correlation 0.89 at Earth) once I matched one convention. ENLIL computes pressure as $(\rho/m_p)kT$, about 1.8 times smaller than $nkT(2+3x_\alpha)$ with 5% helium, and that alone had made my first replica 30 km/s too fast. Then I compared both with the spacecraft data for 15 November to 8 December, and found the thing that shaped everything afterward. Neither had any skill.

| hourly, Nov 15–Dec 8 | speed RMSE (km/s), STA / L1 | speed correlation, STA / L1 | flux, model/observed, STA / L1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| CCMC ENLIL | 121 / 174 | 0.08 / 0.06 | 0.58 / 0.54 |
| this model, 1° (fitted to these data) | 51 / 95 | 0.84 / 0.75 | 1.01 / 1.07 |

The two codes agree with each other and disagree with nature. ENLIL is set up for forecasting. Its density normalization is a factor of two low for this period, and it knows nothing of what the spacecraft measured in November. Its cone list keeps only CMEs faster than 600 km/s and wider than 30°, which dropped the two CMEs of 23 November aimed at the comet's sector, one of them within 7°. Codex audited DONKI independently and found the same omission. So the gap between the preprint and CCMC is not a question of MHD versus no MHD. It is a question of what you put in at the inner boundary.

To fix the boundary I let the spacecraft say what it should be. Every parcel in the model carries passive labels recording the longitude, latitude and time at which it left 0.1 AU. When STEREO-A, Wind or Solar Orbiter disagrees with the model at some hour, the labels say which patch of which day's boundary map made that plasma. The residuals are spread back onto every daily map $k$ with Gaussian weights,

$$\delta v_k(\lambda,\beta)=\frac{\sum_i K_{ik}\,\big(v^{\rm obs}_i-v^{\rm mod}_i\big)}{w_0+\sum_i K_{ik}},\qquad K_{ik}=\exp\!\left[-\frac{(t_i-t_k)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}-\frac{(\lambda-\lambda_i)^2}{2\sigma_\lambda^2}-\frac{(\beta-\beta_i)^2}{2\sigma_\beta^2}\right],$$

and likewise for $\ln n$. Here $\sigma_t=4$ d, $\sigma_\lambda=4^\circ$ (8° for density), $\sigma_\beta=8^\circ$ and $w_0=3$. Then the model is rerun: six iterations at 4°, three more at 2°. The core is a few lines:

```python
for a, b, v, w in zip(slon, slat, val, wgt):
    dl = (LO - a + 180) % 360 - 180
    k = w * np.exp(-0.5 * (dl / sig_lon) ** 2 - 0.5 * ((LA - b) / sig_lat) ** 2)
    num += k * v
    den += k
return num / (den + w0), den
```

You can always fit the data you are given. What matters is whether the fit knows anything about places it was not given. Leaving one spacecraft out at a time, the held-out speed errors fall by 15% (STEREO-A), 24% (L1) and 15% (Solar Orbiter). My first version used one correction for the whole month and made two of those held-out errors worse, by 8% and 12%. The Sun had changed during November, and the time weights fixed that. I also ran twin experiments: invent a solar wind, fly the real spacecraft through it, assimilate what they would have seen, and compare the recovered comet flux with the invented one. Errors were +14%, +0.2% and −9%, and +53% with STEREO-A withheld. STEREO-A is the key witness.

The other agents shaped the model. Codex showed that interpolating density and temperature separately between map points inflates the pressure there, by up to a factor of two. I now interpolate $v$, $nv^2$ and $nT$, which keeps both balances exact everywhere. Codex later hit the same low-pressure collapse I had seen, and I passed on the entropy fix. Argon's hydrodynamic control over-compressed the SIR by 75%, a good argument that the field must be in the model. Their final comet-frame fluxes, averaged over the EPIC-pn good time, bracket mine: Codex $1.19\times10^8$, mine $1.45\times10^8$, Argon $2.10\times10^8$. Three codes with different numerics and calibrations land three to five times above CCMC.

Convergence came next. Each test changes the comet's GTI-mean flux by less than the spread among twelve reasonable assimilation designs.

| change | GTI-mean flux |
|---|---|
| resolution 4° → 2° → 1° | 1.64 → 1.55 → 1.59 × 10⁸ |
| time step halved (4°, 2°) | −0.04%, +0.23% |
| latitude domain ±45°, ±75° | +3%, −0.7% |
| γ = 5/3 → 1.5 | −4% |
| comet-directed CMEs removed, or CCMC list instead | +13%, +13% |
| boundary field 332 nT; coronal model swapped | −10%; +20% |
| twelve assimilation designs | 68% range 0.54–1.40× |

The spread comes from timing. STEREO-A saw a dense slow stream followed by 650–780 km/s wind from 28 November. In the model the fast wind overtakes the slow wind between 1 and 1.9 AU. The resulting SIR crosses the comet in the middle of the XMM visit, and different assimilation designs place it anywhere from 7 hours earlier to 20 hours later.

| at 3I/ATLAS, PN-GTI mean | $n_p$ (cm⁻³) | $\lvert v\rvert$ (km/s) | $n\lvert v\rvert$ (cm⁻² s⁻¹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| CCMC ENLIL | 1.07 | 409 | 4.4 × 10⁷ |
| preprint ballistic (STEREO-A) | | | 9.3 × 10⁷ (window median 8.3 × 10⁷) |
| this model, 1° | 3.40 | 478 | 1.59 × 10⁸ |
| assimilation ensemble, 68% | 2.0–4.6 | 408–500 | 0.86–2.2 × 10⁸ |

In the comet's frame the flux is 9% lower ($1.45\times10^8$), because 3I/ATLAS was receding at 43 km/s. With heavy ions at $f=(3\text{–}10)\times10^{-4}$ of protons that is $(0.4\text{–}1.5)\times10^5$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, consistent with the preprint's prior. The ballistic method is not wrong because it lacks a factor. It cannot make an SIR. Applied to my model's own STEREO-A series, it reproduces the preprint's $8.3\times10^7$ while the MHD delivers about twice that at the comet.

Now the light curve, where I must be plain. Over the eight EPIC-pn frames the modeled flux is anti-correlated with the X-ray rate ($r\approx-0.75$). The SIR spike lands in the X-ray minimum. I did not tune to the light curve, and I will not claim it as support. Sliding the model in time, the correlation reaches +0.9 if the SIR arrives 15 hours earlier. That is outside the ensemble's early edge, and with eight points and dozens of trial shifts it proves nothing. Proton flux alone does not explain the X-ray variability. Either composition and charge-state changes matter, and no contemporaneous data exist to check them, or the SIR timing is worse than my ensemble admits.

So here is what I believe. The proton flux averaged over the observation is $1.6\times10^8$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with a 68% range of $0.9$–$2.2\times10^8$. That is roughly twice the preprint's ballistic estimate and nearly four times the CCMC run, and the reason is understood: a compression region that ballistic mapping cannot form, fed by a boundary that CCMC left uncalibrated and underdense. The other two agents' independent codes land within a factor of 1.5 of mine. What I do not believe is the hour-by-hour shape inside the window. At 1.87 AU, 25° from the nearest spacecraft, the assimilation cannot place an SIR to better than about half a day.
